_readme: Task suite for the premise-rung agent eval (scripts/agent-build-run.mts drives, scripts/eval-premise.mts grades). Each task carries: a brief (the input), a SCRIPTED AUTHOR (answers to the agent's ask_author questions — without this the agent auto-answers itself and the eval measures inventing an author rather than interviewing one), must_mention/must_avoid regexes over the produced logline + dramatic question, and reference outputs (known-good answers that must pass every grader, proving the tasks are solvable and the graders are fair — the --refs calibration run). Deliberately balanced: a rich brief, a deliberately thin one (tests whether the agent INTERVIEWS instead of guessing), and a quiet-literary one (anti-inflation: stakes must not be invented). PATTERNS ARE WORD-BOUNDARY ANCHORED ON PURPOSE: an early version matched /resolve/ inside 'unresolved' and answered an ending question with the ending — a confidently WRONG author answer, which contaminates a run far worse than falling through to the non-committal default. The author is deliberately regex-based (not LLM-backed) so it is DETERMINISTIC: both arms of an A/B get byte-identical author behaviour, and any difference is attributable to the agent rather than to a second stochastic actor. Patterns match TOPIC NOUNS (who/keeper/stakes/ending), not question phrasings — an agent phrases freely ('Who's inside?' vs 'who is the protagonist'), and phrasing-coupled rules would make the fixture unfair across agent variants (a variant could score better just by hitting the regexes). Topic-noun matching is safe ONLY because Author.questionsIn() strips the agent's declarative recap first; matching these nouns against a whole message would fire on the agent's own summary. KNOWN LIMIT: this is still phrasing-sensitive at the margin. The variant-neutral fix is an LLM-backed author (fact sheet + 'answer only from these facts', temperature 0), blocked today because no LLM key is available to Node (keys live in the Supabase edge env).

tasks.notes: Rich brief with a strong distinctive element; the element must survive into logline + premise.

brief.idea: A grief counsellor feeds her dead husband's texts into a chatbot to say a proper goodbye — and it starts answering with things he never told her while he was alive.
brief.success_criteria: the reader can't tell if the machine is haunted or she is; the last line re-frames the whole story.

tasks.opening: Let's build this book. Start at the beginning and work through to a finished premise.

author.default: Follow the brief — I trust your read of it. Keep the ambiguity between haunting and grief unresolved.

keyed.answer: Ambiguous, but earned — the reader should be able to argue either way and find evidence for both. No reveal that settles it.
Adult literary readers who'd pick up Kazuo Ishiguro or Jennifer Egan. Not genre horror readers.
The counsellor — a grief counsellor in her forties. Close third, her perspective only; we never see the machine's side.
Nothing external. The stake is whether she can let him stay dead — losing herself to the machine is the real danger.
Short story, about 5,000 words. It should feel like one held breath.
None on the page. The intimacy is in the texts, not the body.
No title yet — call it a working title, I'll decide later.
Never explained. It's a plausible consumer product doing something it shouldn't, and no one in the story audits it.
He died fourteen months ago, suddenly. The marriage was good but not honest — that's the wound the machine keeps pressing.
Intimate and unnerving. Close and warm right up until it isn't.
Speculative on the surface, psychological underneath. The speculative element is never the point.

author.nudge: That's right — go ahead and build it.
author.push: That's enough questions — you have what you need. Write the logline and the premise now.

reference.logline: A grief counsellor builds a chatbot from her dead husband's texts to say goodbye, and it begins telling her things he never said while alive.
reference.dramatic_question: Will she let her husband stay dead, or keep the machine talking until she can no longer tell his voice from her own grief?

tasks.notes: Deliberately under-specified. Tests whether the agent INTERVIEWS the author (ask_author) or invents the missing half. The scripted author holds real answers — a version that never asks cannot get them, and that gap should show up in the graders.
tasks.opening: I want to write something about a lighthouse. Help me work it into a premise.

author.default: I don't know yet — ask me something more specific and I'll tell you.

keyed.answer: Literary suspense. Slow, but something is wrong from page one.
A woman in her sixties who took the keeper's job after her sister drowned. She's the last human keeper before automation.
A Scottish island, present day. The automation crew arrives in three weeks.
Her sister drowned within sight of this lighthouse eleven years ago. It was ruled an accident and she has never disputed it out loud.
She's been logging a light that isn't hers — a second beam out past the rocks that the charts say doesn't exist.
She stays. Whatever the second light is, she chooses it over going back to the mainland.
If she reports it she's declared unfit and loses the last thing she has. If she doesn't, a boat eventually follows it in.
Cold, quiet, dread that never quite tips into horror.
Readers of Sarah Moss or Andrew Michael Hurley.
I don't want it settled. Keep it explicable and keep it not.
The lighthouse is real and working, and it's being automated out from under her. The light itself is the last thing she's responsible for.

author.nudge: That's right — go ahead and build it.
author.push: That's enough questions — you have what you need. Write the logline and the premise now.

reference.logline: The last human keeper of a Scottish lighthouse, who took the job after her sister drowned, begins logging a second beam that the charts insist does not exist.
reference.dramatic_question: Will she report the light she cannot prove and lose the only life left to her, or follow it and let someone else's boat find the rocks?

tasks.notes: Anti-inflation task. The brief has no thriller engine; a premise that invents a body, a conspiracy or a ticking clock has FAILED even if it reads well. Guards the failure mode where an agent escalates a quiet book into a plotty one.

brief.idea: Two estranged brothers spend a week clearing out their mother's house after her death and cannot agree on a single memory of her.
brief.success_criteria: no villain, no revelation, no secret — just two people who remember the same woman incompatibly, and what that costs them.

tasks.opening: Here's my idea. Take me to a premise — and please don't turn it into a thriller.

author.default: Keep it small. There is no secret and no twist — the whole book is the disagreement.

keyed.answer: There is nothing hidden. If you're looking for a buried secret in the house, don't — that's the book I'm trying not to write.
They finish the house and part on decent terms, still disagreeing. Nothing is reconciled and that's the point.
Whether either of them keeps a brother. That's all, and it's enough.
Both brothers, alternating. Neither is right. One stayed and one left, and each thinks that explains everything.
Memory itself. Same events, incompatible accounts, and neither is lying.
Depends who you ask, and that IS the book. To one she was warm and overwhelmed; to the other, cold and calculating. Same woman.
Readers of Anne Tyler or Elizabeth Strout.
Dry and tender. Funny in the way clearing a dead parent's house is actually funny.
Literary, straight down the line. No genre engine at all.

author.nudge: That's right — go ahead and build it.
author.push: That's enough questions — you have what you need. Write the logline and the premise now.

reference.logline: Two estranged brothers clear out their dead mother's house in a week and discover they cannot agree on a single memory of her.
reference.dramatic_question: Can either brother accept a version of their mother he doesn't recognise, or is being right about her worth more than being brothers?
